title: Correcting Predictions
hook: Start with what similar cases have done. Then adjust for what makes this one different. That is the whole correction.
counterintuition: The most common error in prediction is not the failure to think carefully about the specific case. It is the failure to start with what similar cases have actually done. Case-specific reasoning is valuable; it is the adjustment, not the anchor. A prediction that starts from intuition about the specific case and never consults the distribution of similar past cases does not use the base rate as a guide. It uses the inside view as a substitute for an anchor it never established.
tryThisNow: Before your next prediction, write: the base rate for similar past cases; what makes this case different. Start at the base rate. Adjust by the amount that difference justifies. No difference? Stay at the base rate.
keyTakeaway: Reference class forecasting anchors a prediction to the base rate of similar past cases before case-specific adjustment; the base rate constrains how far intuition can drift without specific justification.

breakdown.fastRead: A single-point prediction can be improved by a two-step process: identify the reference class distribution for similar past cases, then adjust from that base rate for the specific features of the current case. The outside view is the anchor; the inside view is the adjustment. Reversing this order, or skipping the base rate entirely, leaves the prediction as noisy as unstructured intuition. Two analysts estimating the same startup exit probability without a base rate anchor may produce estimates 30 points apart; anchored to a reference class, the same analysts narrow to 6 points apart. The base rate does not replace case-specific knowledge; it constrains how far each predictor can drift from the historical record without a specific justification.
breakdown.deepRead:
The planning fallacy is the tendency to predict project outcomes based on the inside view, what we know about this specific project, while ignoring the outside view, how similar projects have actually performed. Reference class forecasting is the correction: start with how similar projects have performed, then adjust for what is genuinely distinctive about this one. The discipline is in starting with the outside view, not in ignoring the inside view.

The improvement in prediction accuracy from reference class anchoring is not primarily about the accuracy of any single prediction. It is about the consistency of predictions across predictors who hold similar case-specific information. When two analysts start from the same base rate, their case-specific adjustments are made from the same anchor, and their estimates converge. When the same analysts start from pure case-specific intuition, they start from different implicit anchors, and their estimates diverge. The base rate does not tell the analysts the answer; it tells them where to start, and a shared starting point constrains the range of where they can end up. The spread between anchored estimates reflects genuine disagreement about case-specific features; the spread between unanchored estimates reflects both that disagreement and the noise of different implicit starting points.

The reference class is almost always definable. The question is what population of past cases shares enough relevant characteristics to constitute a meaningful distribution. Stage, sector, and revenue range for startup exit probability. Processing stage, country of origin, and documentation completeness for resettlement timelines. Scope, complexity, and team size for software delivery estimates. Defining the reference class is the most consequential step in the forecasting process, because it determines what the anchor will be.

A prediction that skips the reference class is not a forecast. It is an inside view with a number attached to it.
breakdown.fullRead:
Mercer and Ashford are two analysts at the same venture capital firm, reviewing the same portfolio company. Without a reference class, their 5-year exit probability estimates come in at 65 percent and 35 percent, a 30-point gap. Both analysts have access to the same deal memo, the same management team information, and the same sector data. The spread is noise: different implicit anchors producing different numbers for the same company.

With a reference class, the conversation changes. Both analysts first look up the historical 5-year exit rate for companies at the same stage, in the same sector, with the same revenue range. The base rate for that reference class is 38 percent. Now both analysts are adjusting from the same starting point. Mercer thinks the management team quality justifies a modest upward revision. Ashford thinks the product differentiation also supports a slight upward adjustment. Their anchored estimates come in at 41 and 47 percent, a 6-point gap. The base rate did not replace their case-specific knowledge; it constrained how far either analyst could drift from the historical record without a documented justification for doing so.

The planning fallacy runs through every prediction domain where inside-view intuition is permitted to bypass the outside view entirely. Project managers predict delivery timelines based on this project's specific features while ignoring how similar projects have actually performed. Caseworkers estimate resettlement processing timelines based on this case's specific circumstances while ignoring the distribution of completion times for comparable cases at the same stage. Real estate agents recommend listing prices based on this property's specific features while ignoring the comparable sale distribution. Each version of the error is structurally the same: the inside view starts the process and the outside view never enters.

For the most important prediction your organization makes regularly, does everyone who makes that prediction start from the same base rate distribution? If the answer is no, your organization's predictions are being made from different starting points; and that difference in starting points is producing noise that would disappear if the reference class were agreed upon before anyone picked a number. The reference class is not the answer. It is the argument you must defeat to justify a different answer.

In a resettlement agency, caseworkers' unanchored timeline estimates for 30 cases at the same processing stage range from 4 to 14 months, a 10-month inter-caseworker spread. When the same caseworkers are provided with the historical completion time distribution for cases in the same stage, country-of-origin category, and documentation completeness level before making their estimates, the spread narrows to 3 months. The base rate did not tell the caseworkers the answer; it told them where to start and where to explain if they were departing. The documentation of departures is the mechanism that converts noise into accountable adjustment.

In hurricane forecasting, the order of operations matters as much as the information used. When forecasters began with dynamic model output and adjusted for climatological expectations, average inter-model track spread at 72 hours was 95 nautical miles across a season of tracked storms. When the process was reversed, forecasters first established the climatological track distribution for the storm's environmental analogs before integrating dynamic model output, average spread fell to 68 nautical miles. The 28 percent reduction did not represent a reduction in genuine physical uncertainty about storm tracks. It represented the model-specific noise that had been adding to spread because each model was implicitly starting from a different climatological baseline. Standardizing the starting point removed that component of spread without touching the genuine uncertainty.

In software delivery estimation, an organization that requires teams to look up the historical delivery distribution for comparable projects before estimating reduces inter-team spread from 6.8 weeks to 3.2 weeks for similar scope projects. The teams whose estimates departed from the reference class median were required to document the specific feature justifying the departure. That documentation is the audit trail showing which departures were noise and which were information. A departure from the reference class median with a documented case-specific reason is an adjustment; a departure without a documented reason is noise masquerading as judgment. The reference class requirement reveals which departures are which.

In environmental remediation cost estimation, the same principle applies at a different scale. Project engineers estimating costs for matched contamination profiles produced a $2.7 million inter-estimator spread without reference class anchoring; with a historical portfolio base rate as the anchor, spread narrowed to $0.9 million. Strathmore, the project director, noted the asymmetry in departures: estimators who departed from the reference class in the anchored condition could identify specific site features justifying the departure; estimators who departed in the unanchored condition largely could not. The reference class base rate did not improve the accuracy of site-specific engineering assessment. It exposed the difference between engineers who were departing for documented reasons and engineers who were departing because they had started from a different implicit anchor.

Reference class forecasting does not promise accuracy. It promises consistency. Two predictors who start from the same base rate and have access to the same case-specific information will produce more similar predictions than two predictors who start from implicit intuitive anchors. The spread between their anchored estimates is a measure of genuine case-specific disagreement. The spread between their unanchored estimates is a mixture of that disagreement and the noise of different starting points. Only by anchoring to a shared base rate is it possible to separate the two, and to know whether the remaining spread reflects real information or unmeasured noise.

memorableLines.text: The outside view is the anchor; the inside view is the adjustment.
memorableLines.why: Captures the two-step correction in the most compressed possible form. The semicolon is doing essential work.

memorableLines.text: Reference class forecasting is the correction: start with how similar projects have performed, then adjust for what is genuinely distinctive about this one.
memorableLines.why: States the correction concisely enough to be actionable and specifically enough to avoid being platitudinous.

memorableLines.text: The reference class is not the answer. It is the argument you must defeat to justify a different answer.
memorableLines.why: Reframes the base rate as a burden-of-proof mechanism rather than a constraint, which is a more accurate and more motivating description of how it functions.

examples.title: The 30-Point Gap
examples.scenario: "Sixty-five percent," Mercer says, looking up from the deal memo. Ashford's number is 35. The managing partner sets both estimates on the table: the same company, the same information, 30 points apart. Both analysts built from the inside view, the management team quality, the product differentiation, the sector tailwind. Neither looked up the historical 5-year exit rate for companies at the same stage, in the same sector, with the same revenue range before arriving at a number. The reference class base rate for that population is 38 percent. With it as the anchor, Mercer adjusts to 47 and Ashford to 41. Six points apart, both departures from the base rate documented by specific case features each analyst can name.
examples.whatToDo: When deploying reference class forecasting in an investment committee, define the reference class elements before analysts submit estimates: stage, sector, and revenue range. Require each analyst to document the base rate for that reference class before making any case-specific adjustment. Require documentation of any departure from the base rate that exceeds a threshold. The documentation converts noise, unexplained departure from the historical record, into accountable judgment supported by named case-specific features.
examples.whyItMatters: The 30-point unanchored gap is not a disagreement about the company; it is a measurement of how far two analysts drift when they start from implicit intuitive anchors rather than a shared historical baseline. The 6-point anchored gap is a disagreement about the company. Only the second type of disagreement is informative. Reference class anchoring does not eliminate disagreement; it separates the informative kind from the noise kind.

examples.title: Where to Start
examples.scenario: The conference room holds fifteen caseworkers and one spreadsheet on the projector. Claverdale, the case management director, pulls up the comparison: unanchored timeline estimates for 30 matched cases at the same processing stage, ranging from 4 to 14 months across caseworkers. Then the second column: the same 30 cases, the same caseworkers, after each caseworker was provided with the historical completion time distribution for cases in the same processing stage, country-of-origin category, and documentation completeness level before making their estimate. The spread in the second column runs from 7 to 10 months. Three months instead of ten. The historical distribution median was 8 months, with 80th percentile at 12. The base rate did not tell the caseworkers the answer; it told them where to start.
examples.whatToDo: When designing a timeline estimation process for caseworkers or project managers, define the reference class before the estimation session: what combination of case characteristics determines which historical completion times are relevant? Provide the historical distribution for that reference class as the first input in the estimation process, not as a check on an estimate already made. The sequence matters: base rate first, case-specific adjustment second, produces a different and more consistent result than case-specific assessment first, base rate check second.
examples.whyItMatters: A 10-month inter-caseworker spread for cases at the same processing stage is not a finding about case complexity. It is a finding about the absence of a shared starting point. Caseworkers who started from different implicit anchors produced estimates 10 months apart for comparable cases. Caseworkers who started from the same historical distribution produced estimates 3 months apart. The 7-month reduction represents noise that was entirely a product of starting from different implicit baselines rather than from the documented historical record.

examples.title: Before the Models
examples.scenario: Dunbar, the national hurricane center forecast quality director, reviews the season-long comparison after the final storm of the year. Two forecasting protocols were run in parallel across 12 tracked storms. Protocol one: forecasters began with dynamic model output and adjusted for climatological expectations afterward. Average inter-model track spread at 72 hours was 95 nautical miles. Protocol two: forecasters first established the climatological track distribution for each storm's environmental analogs, then integrated dynamic model output as an adjustment. Average spread fell to 68 nautical miles. The 28 percent reduction did not reflect a reduction in genuine physical uncertainty about storm tracks. It reflected the model-specific noise that disappeared when all models started from the same climatological baseline rather than from different implicit assumptions.
examples.whatToDo: When designing a multi-model forecasting protocol, specify the order of operations before any model output is examined: establish the climatological reference distribution for the storm's environmental analogs first, commit to that base rate, then incorporate dynamic model output as adjustment. The order matters because examining model output first implicitly anchors each model's climatological assumptions to its own internal baseline, while examining the climatological distribution first provides a shared anchor that exposes which models are departing and by how much.
examples.whyItMatters: The 28 percent spread reduction when the order of operations was reversed is not evidence that climatological data is more accurate than dynamic models. It is evidence that a shared baseline reduces inter-model noise without reducing genuine physical uncertainty. The remaining 72 nautical miles of average spread after the protocol change represents actual uncertainty about storm tracks; the 27 nautical miles removed by the protocol change was noise in the starting point, not signal about the storm.

examples.title: Comparable Distribution
examples.scenario: What would happen if every listing agent were required to establish the comparable sale distribution before making a listing price recommendation? Hadlow, the real estate brokerage quality director, runs the test on 25 matched properties. Unanchored recommendations, built from each agent's inside-view assessment of the property's specific features, range from $340,000 to $420,000 on average across agents, an $80,000 inter-agent spread. After agents establish the comparable distribution for the same neighborhood, size range, and condition tier before making their recommendation, median $375,000, 10th to 90th percentile $350,000 to $400,000, recommendations range from $365,000 to $390,000. A $25,000 inter-agent spread. The comparable distribution does not tell agents the right price; it tells them where the burden of proof falls for any recommendation outside the range.
examples.whatToDo: When designing a listing price recommendation process, require agents to document the comparable distribution before submitting a recommendation. Define the reference class elements explicitly: neighborhood, size range, condition tier. Require agents who recommend outside the comparable range to document the specific property feature that justifies the departure. This converts the reference class from a suggested starting point to a formal anchor that agents must explicitly depart from with documented reasons.
examples.whyItMatters: An $80,000 inter-agent spread for properties in the same neighborhood and size range is not a finding about property complexity. It is a finding about the absence of a shared starting point. The comparable distribution reduces the spread to $25,000 not by constraining agent judgment but by giving that judgment a shared reference point to depart from. The remaining $25,000 spread reflects genuine agent disagreement about property-specific features; the $55,000 removed by anchoring reflects noise in implicit starting points.

examples.title: Historical Portfolio as Anchor
examples.scenario: The estimating room has maps and contamination profiles pinned to the board. Strathmore, the project director, presents two columns of cost estimates for 20 matched site profiles: same contamination type, site area, and remediation technology. Unanchored estimates from the firm's senior engineers range from $2.1 million to $4.8 million per project, a $2.7 million spread. After engineers first establish the historical cost distribution from the firm's own portfolio for projects in the same contamination-technology-area class, median $3.2 million, 25th to 75th percentile $2.8 million to $3.7 million, estimates range from $2.9 million to $3.8 million, a $0.9 million spread. The engineers whose anchored estimates departed from the median could identify specific site features justifying the departure. The engineers whose unanchored estimates departed largely could not.
examples.whatToDo: When introducing reference class anchoring to an estimation team, use the organization's own historical portfolio as the reference distribution rather than external benchmarks. The firm's own data controls for firm-specific cost drivers, making the reference class more relevant and more credible to the estimators who will use it. Require engineers whose estimates depart from the historical median by more than a threshold to document the specific site feature justifying the departure. Document departures as part of the project record.
examples.whyItMatters: The asymmetry Strathmore observed is the key finding: engineers departing from the reference class in the anchored condition could name the specific site feature making the current project more or less expensive than the historical median; engineers departing in the unanchored condition largely could not. That asymmetry reveals that unanchored departures were noise, starting-point variation with no case-specific justification, while anchored departures were information. Reference class anchoring does not eliminate large estimates; it converts unexplained large estimates into explained ones or eliminates them.

examples.title: Before and After the Reference Class
examples.scenario: You compare two eras in your engineering organization's estimation process. In the inside-view era, teams estimate delivery time based on their assessment of the current project's specific features. Inter-team spread for comparable scope projects averages 6.8 weeks. Teams whose estimates are high explain them as reflecting specific technical risks; teams whose estimates are low explain them as reflecting their familiarity with the technology stack. In the reference class era, teams first look up the historical delivery distribution for the organization's projects in the same scope, complexity, and team-size class before making their estimate. The reference class median for the relevant project class is 18 weeks. Teams whose estimates depart from that median are required to document the specific project feature making their case different. Inter-team spread averages 3.2 weeks. The estimates that depart from the reference class median now have named justifications attached.
examples.whatToDo: When transitioning an estimation process to reference class anchoring, start by building the historical distribution from the organization's own project archive before changing any team's estimation workflow. The reference class must be defined before teams see it, or teams will select the reference class to match their intuitive estimate. Define the scope, complexity, and team-size classification criteria in advance. Train teams on the two-step process: base rate first, case-specific adjustment second, with documented justification for any departure above a threshold.
examples.whyItMatters: The reduction from 6.8 to 3.2 weeks of inter-team spread is not a reduction in genuine uncertainty about project delivery. It is a reduction in the noise produced by teams starting from different implicit baselines. The 3.2-week spread that remains is information: it reflects real disagreement about what makes the current project different from the reference class. The 3.6 weeks removed by the reference class requirement was noise that disappeared when teams were required to share a starting point. Your organization's delivery planning is more consistent in the reference class era not because the teams know more, but because they are starting from the same place.

questions.prompt: What role does the base rate play in reference class forecasting?
choices: The base rate replaces case-specific judgment, producing a prediction that is independent of the predictor's individual knowledge.
The base rate serves as the anchor from which case-specific adjustments are made, constraining how far individual predictions can drift without specific justification.
The base rate sets the ceiling of the prediction range, with case-specific factors used to move the estimate downward toward the most likely value.
questions.explanation: The base rate is the anchor, not the answer. Case-specific information provides the adjustment from that anchor. When two predictors start from the same base rate, their remaining disagreement reflects genuine case-specific differences rather than the noise of different implicit starting points.

questions.prompt: A venture capital fund wants to reduce inter-analyst noise in exit probability estimates for portfolio companies. Which reference class elements should define the base rate distribution?
choices: Company stage, sector, and revenue range: the historical exit rate for companies matching those characteristics provides the base rate anchor before company-specific adjustments.
The fund's own prior exit rate, adjusted for the current macroeconomic environment and the current management team's track record.
The most comparable public market valuations in the same sector, adjusted downward for the liquidity discount applicable to private companies.
questions.explanation: Stage, sector, and revenue range define a meaningful reference class because they capture the characteristics most predictive of exit probability at a population level. The fund's own exit rate is too small a sample to be a reliable base rate, and public comparables introduce a different asset class.

questions.prompt: A resettlement agency case management director wants to reduce inter-caseworker spread in timeline estimates. Which two-step process should caseworkers follow?
choices: First estimate the timeline from case-specific features; then consult the historical median as a reasonableness check and adjust if the estimate falls outside two standard deviations.
First collect all available case documentation; then assign a timeline based on the combined assessment of the caseworker and a senior supervisor.

First look up the historical completion time distribution for cases in the same processing stage, country-of-origin category, and documentation completeness level; then adjust from that base rate for the specific case's distinguishing features.
questions.explanation: The correct sequence is outside view first, inside view second. Consulting the historical distribution before making the case-specific estimate gives the estimate a shared starting point. Using the historical median as a post-hoc reasonableness check does not prevent different implicit anchors from producing different starting points.

questions.prompt: Two real estate agents given the same property produce recommendations of $340,000 and $420,000 without comparable data. The same agents, after establishing the comparable sale distribution, produce recommendations of $365,000 and $390,000. What explains the narrower spread in the second condition?
choices: The comparable distribution provides additional factual information about the property that agents could not infer from inspection alone, reducing genuine uncertainty.
Reviewing comparable data prompts agents to check their reasoning for logical errors, producing more careful estimates after they examine the market evidence.

The comparable distribution gives both agents the same starting point, so their divergence in the second condition reflects only genuine case-specific disagreement rather than the noise of different implicit anchors.
questions.explanation: The comparable distribution does not reveal new facts about the property; it provides a shared starting point. Both agents adjust from the same anchor, so their remaining divergence reflects genuine disagreement about the property's distinctive features. The prior spread included both that disagreement and the noise of starting from different implicit baselines.

questions.prompt: A national hurricane center wants to reduce inter-model track spread by applying reference class forecasting. Which step should forecasters perform first?
choices: Establish the climatological track distribution for storms in similar environmental analog conditions before integrating dynamic model output.
Run all dynamic models independently and compute their average track as the base rate for further adjustment.
Identify the current storm's unique physical features and weight dynamic model output toward the models with the best track record for that storm type.
questions.explanation: The climatological distribution for environmental analogs is the outside view; dynamic model output is the inside view. Starting with the climatological distribution provides a shared baseline that exposes which models are departing from historical norms and by how much. Starting with model output means each model implicitly uses its own internal climatological assumptions as the baseline.

questions.prompt: A hurricane forecast quality director finds that requiring climatological anchoring before dynamic model integration reduces average inter-model spread from 95 to 68 nautical miles across a season. What does the 28 percent reduction measure?
choices: The improvement in individual model accuracy achieved when models are required to start from a shared climatological prior before diverging.
The reduction in genuine physical uncertainty about storm tracks when forecasters incorporate additional historical storm analogs in the forecast process.
The proportion of inter-model spread that was noise from different implicit climatological starting points rather than genuine uncertainty about the storm's physical trajectory.
questions.explanation: The 28 percent reduction represents spread that was produced by models starting from different implicit baselines, not by genuine physical uncertainty. Standardizing the starting point removes that component without changing the genuine uncertainty about storm tracks, which remains in the 68 nautical miles of spread that persists after anchoring.

questions.prompt: A software organization requires teams to look up the delivery time distribution for comparable projects before estimating, and requires documentation for estimates departing from the reference class median. Why does the documentation requirement reduce noise rather than simply constraining estimates?
choices: The documentation requirement converts unexplained departure from the reference class into accountable adjustment supported by a named case-specific reason, preserving genuine case-specific information while removing unexplained spread.
The documentation requirement creates a record allowing managers to identify systematic estimation biases across project teams and apply corrections in planning assumptions.
The documentation requirement reduces noise by introducing a social cost for departing from the base rate, which discourages overconfident estimates without eliminating case-specific judgment.
questions.explanation: Documentation does not eliminate departures from the reference class; it distinguishes departures with case-specific justification from departures without one. The first type is information; the second is noise. The documentation requirement converts the second type into either an accountable adjustment or an eliminated departure, leaving only the genuine case-specific disagreement.

questions.prompt: An engineering project manager estimates remediation costs at $4.8 million for a site profile whose reference class median is $3.2 million. What should the manager do to apply reference class forecasting correctly?
choices: Revise the estimate downward to the reference class median, since a significant unexplained departure from the historical distribution signals overconfident inside-view estimation.
Document the specific site features that justify the departure from the $3.2 million median before finalizing the estimate.
Average the intuitive estimate and the reference class median to produce a balanced estimate incorporating both inside-view and outside-view information.
questions.explanation: Reference class forecasting does not require estimates to equal the median; it requires departures to be justified by named case-specific features. An estimate of $4.8 million is valid if the manager can identify the specific site characteristics that make the project more expensive than the historical reference class. The documentation is what converts the departure from noise into information.

questions.prompt: A product team estimates delivery at 28 weeks based on the current project's technical complexity. The reference class median for similar scope projects is 18 weeks. The team argues their inside-view analysis justifies the departure. What is the most important question to ask before accepting this estimate?
choices: Whether the reference class median was computed from projects with comparable team size and budget, which are the primary drivers of delivery variance.

Whether the team can articulate the specific features that make this project genuinely different from the reference class, and whether those features would predictably add ten weeks rather than some other amount.
Whether the team's inside-view analysis was reviewed by an external estimator who is not subject to the planning fallacy's tendency to inflate project duration estimates.
questions.explanation: The reference class provides a burden of proof: the team must be able to name the specific features that make this project different from the historical median and explain why those features add ten weeks rather than some other amount. A vague claim that the project is technically complex does not constitute a specific justification for a 10-week departure from the reference class.

reviewCards.front: What is the two-step structure of reference class forecasting?
reviewCards.back: First, identify the reference class distribution for similar past cases and use it as the base rate anchor. Second, adjust from that base rate for the specific features of the current case. The outside view is the anchor; the inside view is the adjustment. Reversing the order, or skipping the base rate, leaves the prediction as noisy as unstructured intuition.

reviewCards.front: What does the planning fallacy describe, and what is its correction?
reviewCards.back: The planning fallacy is the tendency to predict outcomes based on the inside view of the specific case while ignoring the outside view of how similar cases have actually performed. Reference class forecasting is the correction: start with how similar cases have performed, then adjust for what is genuinely distinctive about this one.

reviewCards.front: Why does starting from the same base rate reduce inter-predictor spread even when predictors have the same case-specific information?
reviewCards.back: Predictors who start from their own implicit anchors introduce noise in addition to genuine case-specific disagreement. Predictors who start from the same base rate share a starting point, so their remaining divergence reflects only genuine disagreement about case-specific features rather than the additional noise of different implicit starting points.

reviewCards.front: What does requiring documentation of reference class departures accomplish?
reviewCards.back: It converts unexplained departure from the base rate into either a named, case-specific justification (information) or an eliminated departure (noise removed). The documentation distinguishes the two types of departure, preserving genuine case-specific judgment while eliminating deviation without justification.

reviewCards.front: What does a reduction in inter-predictor spread after reference class anchoring measure?
reviewCards.back: The proportion of prior spread attributable to noise from different implicit starting points rather than genuine case-specific disagreement. The remaining post-anchoring spread reflects genuine information about what makes cases different; the removed spread was noise that disappeared when predictors shared a starting point.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Anchoring predictions to reference class base rates before applying case-specific adjustments

ifThenPlans.context: You are making a single-point prediction for a decision with similar historical cases
ifThenPlans.plan: Before committing to a number, write down the reference class: the population of past cases that share the relevant characteristics with the current case. Look up the historical distribution for that reference class. Write down the base rate as your starting point. Then write down the specific features of the current case that justify any departure from the base rate. Your final estimate is the base rate plus the adjustment those features justify. If you cannot name the specific features justifying a departure, stay closer to the base rate than your intuition suggests.

ifThenPlans.context: A team or organization makes the same type of prediction repeatedly across different cases or predictors
ifThenPlans.plan: Define the reference class before the prediction cycle begins, not after. Specify which case characteristics determine which historical outcomes are relevant. Provide the historical distribution for that reference class as the first input in the prediction process. Require predictors to document any departure from the base rate with a named case-specific justification. Review departure documentation to distinguish genuine case-specific adjustments from noise in the starting point.

ifThenPlans.context: A predictor's estimate departs significantly from the reference class base rate
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask the predictor to name the specific features of the current case that justify the departure and to quantify how much each feature moves the estimate. If the predictor cannot name specific features, the departure is likely noise rather than information. If the predictor can name specific features, the departure is an accountable adjustment that belongs in the record. Do not accept a general claim that the current case is unusual as a justification; specificity is the test.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Identify the most important recurring prediction your team makes. Before the next instance of that prediction, write down the reference class and look up the historical base rate. Then write down what makes the current case different. Compare your anchored estimate to what your intuitive estimate would have been without the base rate.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, for any prediction you make, write down the base rate before writing down your estimate. After three months, you will have a record showing how far your estimates departed from the base rate and whether those departures were justified by named case-specific features or by nothing you could articulate.
